records.name: Ducts, lobules and the terminal duct lobular unit
records.tldr: Breast ducts connect to milk-producing acini, with supporting tissues around them. This anatomy helps interpret a sample but does not by itself establish cancer.
records.summary:
The breast contains an interconnected duct-lobular epithelial system within connective and fatty tissue. A terminal duct with its associated acini forms a terminal duct lobular unit. Tissue compartments and their proportions matter when interpreting imaging, microscopy or bulk molecular measurements. Histological diagnosis, grade, receptor status and disease extent require their own evidence.

NCI DCEG describes the TDLU as the origin of most breast cancer precursors and cancers. The names ductal and lobular are diagnostic morphology, not proof of an exact ancestral cell. Characteristic loss of E-cadherin in invasive lobular carcinoma reduces cell adhesion; diffuse growth in unconnected lines can make a lesion harder to feel or detect on imaging. The SEER description concerns this growth pattern rather than a universal test result for every lobular tumour.

Male breasts have ducts and may have lobules, but far fewer than female breasts; NCI describes lobular cancer as rare in men. Breast tissue and mammographic density change over life. Greater density is associated with higher breast-cancer risk and can obscure cancers on a mammogram; increasing age and childbearing are associated with lower density, alongside other influences. Mammographic density, TDLU involution and histological diagnosis are different observations.

notes: The terminal duct lobular unit contains a terminal duct and its associated acini. Acini make milk during lactation; ducts carry it towards the nipple. Lobules and larger lobes are different levels of organisation. Their size and abundance vary with physiology and life stage; an illustrative branch count is not a fixed anatomical count. A schematic grouping bracket is an annotation, not a tissue capsule or basement membrane. NCI DCEG describes TDLU involution with physiological ageing and completion of childbearing as reductions in acini per unit and total unit counts. This is an observational normal-tissue description, not a diagnostic rule for an individual.

From a typical normal acinus lumen outward, distinguish luminal epithelial cells, living myoepithelial cells, extracellular basement membrane and surrounding stroma. Stroma includes connective tissue, fat, vessels and immune cells. A basement membrane is neither a cell layer nor the plasma membrane around one cell.

An epithelial marker or abundant epithelial RNA can come from normal epithelium. A sample richer in glands and poorer in stroma can change a bulk measurement without a change within either cell type. Imaging, tissue morphology and protein staining observe different scales; a normal-breast atlas is a reference, not a stand-alone cancer diagnosis.

A quadrant or clock position locates a lesion. It does not identify its ancestral cell, receptor class or invasiveness. Likewise, ductal and lobular diagnostic names do not prove the precise ancestral location, and anatomical luminal position does not assign a molecular luminal subtype. A milk-flow diagram is not a cancer-progression sequence.

Ducts are epithelium-lined channels connected to milk-producing acini in lobules. The TDLU is a tissue unit, not one cell or a molecular subtype. Epithelial tissue can be normal, in situ or invasive: DCIS remains within the ductal boundary, whereas invasion enters surrounding tissue. In a fictional bulk assay, abundant epithelial RNA cannot establish invasion; that distinction needs tissue organisation, not simply epithelial abundance.

Milk ducts and lymphatic drainage are different networks. A quadrant or clock address supplies neither a drainage map nor lineage. Normal-anatomy drawings simplify scale, cell counts and branching; selected source text and captions support the arrangement illustrated, not a diagnosis or a universal number of cells.

In an invented normal-tissue cutaway, a larger duct connects to a terminal duct serving several hollow acini. The selected TDLU includes that terminal duct and its acini, excluding the larger duct. Each duct or acinus has its own epithelial boundary and basement membrane, with stroma around and between these structures. A bracket selects the group without adding a shared capsule. Magnifying one acinus shows a lumen, luminal epithelium, living nucleated myoepithelial cells, extracellular basement membrane and stroma rather than the whole lobule or breast. The branch count and magnification are chosen for the example.

records.name: Myoepithelial cells and the breast basement membrane
records.tldr: Myoepithelial cells are living cells around normal breast ducts and acini; basement membrane is separate extracellular material outside them.
records.summary: These layers help organise normal breast structures and support pathological assessment of invasion. Their location, morphology, staining controls and diagnostic context matter more than a single positive or negative marker.

links.label: Normal and tumor-derived myoepithelial cells differ in their ability to interact with luminal breast epithelial cells for polarity and basement membrane deposition.

notes: Typical normal breast ducts and acini have luminal epithelial cells facing the lumen, an outer living myoepithelial layer, extracellular basement membrane and then stroma. Myoepithelial cells have contractile features that help move milk; they are not the chest muscle. Basement membrane contains matrix proteins such as laminins and type IV collagen, not living cells.

Basement membrane beneath an epithelial structure differs from plasma membrane around one cell. Cell polarity describes different inward and outward organisation. Gudjonsson and colleagues' human-cell culture experiments showed that normal myoepithelial cells or laminin-1 could restore luminal orientation in collagen gels; this is model evidence about organisation, not a demonstrated cancer treatment.

Myoepithelial immunohistochemistry is supporting evidence interpreted with morphology. p63 is nuclear; calponin and smooth muscle myosin heavy chain are cytoplasmic markers. Ask which cells stain, where they stain and whether technical controls work. A failed positive control undermines an apparently absent rim.

Werling and colleagues found gaps around some noninvasive structures, stromal staining with muscle-associated markers and p63 staining in some carcinoma cells. Gusterson and colleagues found basement-membrane proteins in some invasive carcinomas. Neither marker absence nor protein presence alone proves the tissue boundary. Basal-like RNA features also do not establish myoepithelial ancestry.

In Gusterson and colleagues' 1982 tissue study, laminin and type IV collagen were detected in normal breast, benign lesions and grade I invasive carcinomas but were absent from grade II and III infiltrating carcinomas in that study. That historical cohort does not make protein presence proof of an intact noninvasive boundary, or protein absence a universal grade rule.

Werling and colleagues examined 85 breast lesions. In that series, at least focal p63 staining in tumour cells occurred in 11% of cases, while stromal myofibroblasts stained with smooth muscle myosin heavy chain in 8% and calponin in 76%. Some noninvasive structures had gaps. These assay- and cohort-specific observations explain why localisation and controls matter; they are not universal diagnostic accuracy estimates.

CAP's morphology-based histological classification and supporting-marker assessment answer a tissue question. A schematic rim is neither an immunostain result nor a diagnosis; illustrated gaps or colours cannot establish invasion. Interpret the actual tissue architecture and appropriately controlled stains together.

records.name: Breast lymphatic drainage and the axilla
records.tldr: Breast lymphatics carry fluid to regional nodes through variable routes, including the axilla and internal mammary chain.
records.summary: A drainage territory and a sampled node are different things. Anatomical location helps interpret the evidence, but imaging and tissue examination have different roles and limitations. A nodal result applies to the assessed region and method.

links.label: The lymphatic anatomy of the breast and its implications for sentinel lymph node biopsy: a human cadaver study.
CAP invasive breast resection protocol 4.11.0.0, June 2026
NCI sentinel-node biopsy

notes: Lymphatic vessels carry tissue fluid, material and cells to draining nodes. Nodes also participate in immune responses, and enlargement alone does not establish cancer. Drainage pathways vary; they are not a compulsory sequence of cancer spread, and lymphatic spread is not the only route of dissemination.

Axillary levels are locations relative to pectoralis minor: level I is lateral to its lateral border, level II between its borders, and level III medial to its medial border and below the clavicle. Levels are neither overall stages nor proof of involvement.

Keep axillary, intramammary and internal mammary locations distinct. Intramammary nodes are grouped with axillary nodes for breast N staging; ipsilateral internal mammary nodes belong to a separate regional chain. Regional N involvement, including extranodal extension, does not alone establish distant M disease.

Tracer mapping identifies particular draining nodes under the procedure's conditions; an anatomical sketch cannot substitute for mapping. Preserve the sampled region, side, procedure, treatment timing and pathological result. Negative examined axillary nodes do not resolve an indeterminate internal mammary image or survey all regional nodes.

The axilla is the armpit. Superficial and deeper lymphatic routes vary; a map omits many vessels and node groups. It assigns neither a personal first draining node nor a stage. Disease, prior surgery and treatment can affect procedural mapping, so drawn routes cannot replace the actual mapping and pathological record.

In an illustrative front view of the left breast, the sternum lies toward the midline and the axilla toward the side. An intramammary node is shown within breast tissue. Branching dashed routes represent possible lymph flow, without a compulsory sequence through axillary levels I, II and III. A chosen node icon has no assigned sentinel, sampled or tumour-positive status. Tracer mapping identifies procedural sentinels; the sampling and pathology records establish what was removed and what it contained.

records.name: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS)
records.tldr: Ductal carcinoma in situ means abnormal cancer cells remain within breast ducts, without invasion identified in that component.
records.summary:
Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and invasive breast carcinoma describe different tissue relationships. They can coexist, so each component must remain visible in the report. DCIS grade describes microscopic appearance; staging describes extent under a specified system. Individual management requires the complete diagnosis and treatment context, rather than a fixed progression probability inferred from the name.

NCI's Breast Cancer Treatment PDQ estimates that DCIS accounts for about 25% of invasive and noninvasive breast tumours detected by screening. Treatment choices include breast-conserving surgery, usually considered with radiotherapy, or mastectomy; endocrine risk reduction depends on hormone-receptor status and the full clinical setting. Screening detection and the name DCIS do not establish one fixed probability of progression.

TAM-01 studied tamoxifen 5 mg daily for three years against placebo after surgery, with or without irradiation, in 500 women with breast intraepithelial neoplasia; 69% had DCIS. Its 10-year report found fewer breast events in that mixed study population. It did not compare 5 mg with standard-dose tamoxifen. Active-monitoring programmes ask a different question: COMET's two-year noninferiority result concerned selected women aged at least 40 with hormone-receptor-positive, grade 1 or 2 DCIS, and does not establish long-term equivalence for all DCIS. LORD separately studies active surveillance in selected screen-detected low-risk DCIS. LORIS was developed to compare surgery with active monitoring in selected low-risk DCIS; its protocol describes a research question, not a result establishing safety for every lesion.

notes: Ductal carcinoma in situ describes malignant epithelial cells within the ductal tissue boundary, without invasion identified in that component. An invasive component can coexist in the same specimen. Reading DCIS present does not cancel a separately reported invasive diagnosis. DCIS may be called precancer, noninvasive breast cancer or stage 0 disease; these terms retain the anatomical distinction and do not guarantee that every lesion has the same future risk.

Grade and extent are separate observations. High-grade DCIS does not establish distant spread. AJCC eighth-edition stage 0 is Tis N0 M0; an associated invasive component requires its own staging assessment. A study confined to DCIS does not establish treatment benefit in invasive triple-negative disease.

Mammographic abnormalities can prompt evaluation, but tissue examination establishes the diagnosis. Preserve the component, specimen and full diagnosis. Neither a schematic boundary nor one marker is a diagnostic test, and the phrase in situ does not predict every lesion's future behaviour.

In the AJCC eighth-edition tables reproduced by NCI, stage 0 is Tis N0 M0. Tis includes DCIS and nipple Paget disease without associated invasive carcinoma or DCIS in the underlying breast parenchyma. When underlying parenchymal carcinoma is present, its characteristics determine classification. A fictional report of invasive carcinoma with associated high-grade DCIS is therefore not stage 0 merely because DCIS is present.

CAP records the invasive and DCIS components separately. The surrounding myoepithelial cells are living cells; basement membrane is extracellular matrix, including proteins studied by Gusterson and colleagues. Their detection is not a stand-alone invasion test. Drawing colours, simplified counts and sizes represent locations rather than grade, stage or an inevitable progression.

records.name: Invasive breast carcinoma of no special type (invasive ductal carcinoma)
aka: Invasive carcinoma of no special type
Invasive ductal carcinoma not otherwise specified
records.tldr: Invasive carcinoma of no special type, still widely called invasive ductal carcinoma, is the ordinary form of breast cancer and by far the most common. The name means the tumour has no special pattern that would put it in one of the rarer types; everything on the main breast cancer page and its receptor subpages is written about this type unless it says otherwise.
records.summary:
The WHO classification uses invasive breast carcinoma of no special type for the large group of adenocarcinomas that cannot be classified as a special histological type; the 2019 edition keeps the term, treats the former medullary, oncocytic, lipid-rich, glycogen-rich, sebaceous and pleomorphic carcinomas as patterns within it, and grades it by the Nottingham system (Tan 2020). It is then divided clinically by oestrogen receptor, progesterone receptor and HER2 status and, in early disease, by genomic assays such as Oncotype DX, which is how the corpus's HR-positive, HER2-positive and triple-negative pages and their subpages are organised.

How it differs from its parent: it is not a subtype so much as the default; the special types on the sibling pages (lobular, tubular, mucinous, cribriform, papillary, secretory, adenoid cystic, apocrine, micropapillary, metaplastic, neuroendocrine) are defined against it and several carry a better or worse prognosis than grade-matched no special type disease.

How common: the most common type of breast cancer (Cancer Research UK); Cancer Research UK gives no percentage and this page does not estimate one.

Treatment: entirely as the parent and its receptor pages describe (surgery, radiotherapy, endocrine therapy, chemotherapy, HER2-directed therapy and immunotherapy by receptor status and stage).

notes: Invasive carcinoma has entered surrounding tissue; distant metastasis is a separate finding. No special type (NST), commonly called invasive ductal carcinoma, is a histological category for invasive breast carcinoma without the defining morphology of a special type. NST does not mean an unknown primary or an absence of molecular features.

Histological type, Nottingham grade, receptor results and stage describe different axes. NST alone establishes neither triple-negative status nor a molecular subtype or prognosis. An associated DCIS component does not negate invasion.

Diagnosis integrates morphology with supporting immunohistochemistry when needed. A myoepithelial stain is not a universal binary invasion test. Limited biopsy may not show the entire lesion; preserve specimen and treatment timing when a larger resection reveals more components. Ductal naming does not prove ancestry in a particular large duct.

Carcinoma is an epithelial malignancy. Invasive ductal carcinoma and infiltrating ductal carcinoma are common names corresponding to the CAP category invasive carcinoma of no special type (ductal); retain the full report wording. A DCIS-only sample has not demonstrated invasion in that sample, while associated DCIS does not cancel separately identified invasion.

SEER's 2013 histology inquiry connects ductal NOS terminology with no special type; the WHO/IARC classification structure lists NST as a category, and CAP supplies current reporting terminology. These naming references do not replace morphology. A diagram comparing in situ and invasive arrangements shows a spatial distinction, not a claim that every lesion must pass through those scenes.

This is the default, and the default is where the receptor result takes over. Invasive carcinoma of no special type is defined by not having a special pattern, so once a report says no special type, or invasive ductal carcinoma, everything that follows is decided by the grade, the stage and the receptors rather than by the type. The sixth edition of the WHO classification (April 2026) moves two groups into this category that used not to be here: mucinous carcinomas that are high grade, oestrogen receptor negative or HER2 positive become carcinoma of no special type with mucin production, and the unified neuroendocrine model the fifth edition applied to the breast is abandoned, with routine neuroendocrine staining of ordinary carcinoma no longer recommended.
